study: Black, Kolesnikova, Sanders & Taylor 2013 (Are Children Normal?)
design: Quasi-experiment / natural experiment. Appalachian coal boom-and-bust used as a localized, exogenous shock to men's lifetime income in coal-rich counties, with non-coal counties as comparison. Three complementary analyses: (1) county-level panel regressions of change in birth rates on lagged change in log earnings with state-year fixed effects, using the change in the value of county coal reserves as an instrument (IV); (2) age-specific fertility rates (ASFRs) for the 1946 cohort, coal vs non-coal counties; (3) cohort-level CEB difference-in-differences across 1935-1960 birth cohorts (boom vs bust cohorts), coal vs non-coal counties.
confounding: some — coal-reserve-value instrument plausibly exogenous and state-year FE absorb secular trends, but boom and bust nearly coincide, male wage shock bundles income + substitution channels, and unobserved local shocks correlated with coal cannot be fully excluded
selection: some — potential selective migration into/out of coal counties; authors show no large selective in-migration of young women (1980 Census) but cannot identify out-migrants or in-migrant tastes
measurement: some — county birth rates rely on imprecise inter-censal population denominators (authors re-run on counts; results similar); CEB for 1951-1960 cohorts is a synthetic-cohort estimate (1990 CEB + 2000 own-children); husband-income is current annual income used as proxy for lifetime income
reporting: low — multiple complementary designs reported, directions and rough magnitudes consistent; some SEs not reported for Table 6 (stated ~0.01-0.04)

study: INTENDED: Cesarini, Lindqvist, Notowidigdo & Ostling, 'Wealth, Health, and Child Development: Evidence from Administrative Data on Swedish Lottery Players' (QJE 2016). ACTUAL FILE CONTENT: Pinkovskiy & Sala-i-Martin, 'Lights, Camera,... Income! Estimating Poverty Using National Accounts, Survey Means, and Lights' (NBER WP 19831, Jan 2014).

confounding: High risk for a C.1.a (income) estimand. Aggregate, non-causal associations; income effect not separable from substitution/price-of-time or uncertainty. Predictors are substantially intercorrelated (unemployment-CCI ~ -0.42; EPU-CCI ~ -0.51; bonds-unemployment >0.4 in Southern Europe; VIF >5.8 when unemployment+bonds combined), so author avoids all-variable models. Country and country-by-year fixed effects and linear time trend included, mitigating fixed confounders but not time-varying omitted variables; purely observational macro correlation.
overall: Credible descriptive macro evidence of a procyclical, negative fertility-unemployment/uncertainty association; NOT fit for identifying the C.1.a pure income-as-normal-good effect. Useful only as CONTEXT and as a negative signpost that routes to C.5.a (economic uncertainty/unemployment).

study: Dettling & Kearney, "House Prices and Birth Rates", J. Public Economics (2014)

confounding: low - idiosyncratic exogenous lottery win plausibly orthogonal to preferences/prices; no pre-trends detected
selection: some - sample is lottery players restricted to wins >=$30k and ages 21-64; winners slightly more single/male, less likely homeowners than average filer, though broadly representative across AGI quartiles
measurement: low - administrative W-2G + tax records; reported vs calculated taxes corr 0.997
reporting: low for outcomes studied, but NOT APPLICABLE to fertility since no fertility outcome exists; cannot infer null-vs-unreported for childbearing

study: Kearney & Wilson, "Male Earnings, Marriageable Men, and Nonmarital Fertility: Evidence from the Fracking Boom", REStat 2018 (NBER WP 23408)
design: Reduced-form panel OLS at PUMA x year level (2,044 PUMAs x 16 years), with PUMA fixed effects, state-by-year effects, and time-varying PUMA controls (sex ratio, log house price, race and education shares). Identification off simulated new fracking production (geology-driven shale-play exposure x year), measured in $1,000 per capita. Also reports an auxiliary IV (production as instrument for per-capita earnings) for comparison to Black et al. 2013.
confounding: Moderate -- house prices and sex ratio controlled and results robust; but shock bundles male earnings with unearned royalty/lease income and female earnings, which cannot be separated, so a pure income effect is not isolated.
selection: Low-Moderate -- high-migration areas (ND, MT) and an outlier PUMA excluded; simulated production purges production-choice endogeneity; retained areas had minimal population change.
measurement: Moderate -- treatment is simulated proxy (corr 0.69 with actual); wages are job-level QWI not individual potential wages; births dated back to conception.
reporting: Low -- marital, non-marital, total, share, and marriage outcomes all reported with extensive robustness and heterogeneity appendix tables.
overall: Moderate -- credible causal estimate of the effect of a local positive economic shock on fertility, but weak for isolating a pure non-labor income effect from the wage/earnings channel.
